# Zero Day

## Chapter Twelve: Disclosure Day

The email sat in Maya Okafor's drafts folder for six hours before she sent it. Ninety days, four hours, and eleven minutes since her first disclosure to Meridian Systems. She'd counted. She'd counted every single day.

She read the draft one final time:

*To: security@meridiansys.com; psirt@meridiansys.com; cert@meridiansys.com*
*Subject: Coordinated Disclosure — CVE Request Pending — MER-2024-0117*

*Per our agreed 90-day coordination window, which expires today at 17:00 EST, Meridian Systems has not released a patch for the authentication bypass vulnerability I reported on March 3rd (tracking ref: MER-2024-0117). This vulnerability affects approximately 2.3 million deployed devices, including medical facility gateways.*

*I have published my findings at the URL below, including a technical write-up and proof-of-concept code. I have redacted the most weaponizable details but note that determined actors will reproduce the exploit within days.*

*I take no pleasure in this. I gave you everything you needed to fix this in three weeks. You chose not to.*

*— Dr. Maya Okafor*
*Independent Security Researcher*

Her finger hovered over the trackpad. Somewhere in Ohio, a hospital was running Meridian gateways. Somewhere in those gateways was the flaw she'd found on a rainy Tuesday, the one that let anyone with a laptop and forty-five seconds walk through the front door of the network as if it were made of tissue paper.

*If I publish and someone exploits it before the patch ships, that's on me.*

*If I don't publish, Meridian ships the fix in v4.2 "eventually," buries the CVE, and 2.3 million devices stay vulnerable for another year.*

She pressed send at 4:58 p.m. Two minutes early. She wasn't a monster.

---

The phone rang at 5:03 p.m.

"Dr. Okafor." The voice was smooth, unhurried, the voice of a man paid by the hour to be reasonable. "Derek Voss, Meridian legal counsel. We've been trying to reach you all week."

"You have my email."

"We do. And I'll be direct with you, because I think you're a reasonable person." A pause, calibrated. "That write-up you just published contains proprietary source code fragments. Our code. Publishing it may constitute a violation of the terms of service your client organization agreed to when purchasing our hardware."

Maya leaned back in her chair. Outside her apartment window, Chicago was turning gold with sunset, oblivious. "The terms of service don't govern security research, Mr. Voss. And the code fragments fall squarely under fair use for interoperability and vulnerability disclosure. DMCA 1201 has an explicit exemption. I checked with a lawyer. A real one."

"Dr. Okafor—"

"Did you call to threaten me, or to tell me the patch is shipping?"

Silence. Then, quieter: "The patch ships in v4.2. Q3."

"Q3 ends September thirtieth. That's seventy-one more days. That's not a patch, that's a press release with a download link that doesn't work yet."

"There are dependencies. Enterprise clients require—"

"Enterprise clients require not being on the front page of the *Tribune* when their patient records walk out the door." She heard him inhale, and cut in before he could deploy whatever he'd prepared. "Mr. Voss. I published responsibly. I coordinated. I extended your window once already, in good faith, when you asked for time to 'validate the findings.' I validated them for you, remember? I sent the working exploit. You used it in your own internal test harness — I know because your test server phoned home to my canary."

Another silence, longer this one.

"Here's what happens next," Maya said. "CISA has been notified. The CVE is in queue — MITRE assigned it an hour ago. The medical ISAC gets my advisory tomorrow morning. And if v4.2 doesn't ship within fourteen days, I publish the unredacted exploit and give a talk about it. There's a conference in Denver with an open CFP."

"You'd burn the bridge," Voss said. "No vendor will work with you again."

"No vendor *has* worked with me. That's rather the point."

She hung up before he could answer. It felt childish the moment she did it, and she didn't care.

---
